title: School WASH education and infrastructure maintenance improve student knowledge and facilities but are insufficient for behavior change
content:
by Gracie Hornsby, Christine Pu, Anvesh Badamikar, Poorva Shekher, Dinesh Bhatt, James Winter, Preksha Gupta, Nikita Purty, Ruhi Saith, Gary L. Darmstadt, Jenna Davis

Improving water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) service delivery in schools (WinS) supports progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals, yet rigorous trials report inconsistent effects on student behavior and health. We examined the individual and combined impacts of WASH education and infrastructure operation and maintenance (O&M) in a four-arm cluster randomized controlled trial (cRCT) across 200 public primary schools of Uttar Pradesh, India. Interventions included a teacher-delivered, play-based WASH curriculum and a third-party O&M service. The Curriculum intervention significantly improved all student WASH knowledge outcomes, whereas O&M alone showed no effect. The O&M intervention yielded significant, sustained improvements in toilet-related infrastructure outcomes, making toilets more likely to be unlocked, clean, functional, and to have water available for anal cleansing. Despite these improvements in knowledge and facility conditions, neither intervention, individually or combined, significantly changed observed rates of student toilet use or handwashing. These findings suggest that while improved curriculum and O&M can improve knowledge and facilities, behavior change in the school context remains a persistent challenge.
